subject: history
title: Indian Independence and Suez
welcome_lead: From the Salt March to the Suez Crisis: empire after two world wars.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on Indian independence 1947 and the Suez Crisis of 1956.
final_note: You have watched the empire unravel.

concepts.def: Founded 1885; under Gandhi from 1920 it led mass civil disobedience for independence.
Gandhi's 1930 protest march to Dandi against the British salt monopoly, mobilising mass non-cooperation.
1942 Congress campaign demanding immediate British withdrawal; suppressed by mass arrests.
1947 division of British India into India and Pakistan; up to 14 million displaced and an estimated million killed.
October-November 1956 conflict after Nasser nationalised the canal; Anglo-French-Israeli action halted by US pressure.
Egyptian president (1956-70) who nationalised the Suez Canal Company on 26 July 1956.

walkthroughs.h2: Why did Britain leave India in 1947?
walkthroughs.body_html: Second World War financial exhaustion left Britain owing India GBP 1.3 billion in sterling balances. The 1942 Quit India movement and 1946 Royal Indian Navy mutiny showed waning legitimacy. Attlee's Labour government accepted independence in February 1947. Mountbatten brought the date forward to 15 August 1947, accepting Partition into India and Pakistan amid catastrophic communal violence.

After Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company on 26 July 1956, Eden secretly colluded with France and Israel (Protocol of Sevres). Israel invaded Sinai on 29 October; Anglo-French paratroopers landed on 5 November. US opposition triggered a run on sterling. Eisenhower withheld IMF support unless Britain withdrew. Forces left in December 1956; Eden resigned in January 1957.

Suez exposed Britain's inability to act independently of the United States, accelerated decolonisation, and damaged sterling's reserve role. Macmillan (Chancellor in 1956) became Prime Minister and oversaw rapid African withdrawal, including the 1960 Wind of Change speech in Cape Town. The crisis is widely regarded as the symbolic end of Britain's great-power status.
